type.display_rule:
Once per page on composed graphics: one element, the largest one. A second use
makes it a body face and it is not one. On the web the opt-in is an attribute,
which also stops the layout requesting the face unless a page asks for it.

canvas.relation_to_web: shares 14 / 30 / 72; not a multiple. See DECISIONS.md B3b

drafting.note:
Annotation is the exception and is deliberate: a dimension line and its text
are text_dim, never the accent. A dimension measures the subject, it is not the
subject, and giving it the accent would spend the accent on a ruler.

override.reason:
The formula gives about 180 at this size. 520 would be busy under a page of body
copy; over a hero it is the point. Prominence comes from the dust count, not from
raising grain — grain is a wash and pushing it greys the whole surface.

meta.source:
Industrial Accents rev A · industrial-design-language.md (441 lines, 16 accents
in its taxonomy, 13 taken forward) · the deck templates and video frames as
measured

rule.title: It means something.
rule.body:
A part number is on a part. A tick scale measures a thing that is on the page.
If the accent points at nothing it is a sticker, and stickers are what the work
must never become.

rule.title: One per screen.
rule.body:
A single accent reads as intent. Three read as a theme. The unit of "one" is
different on each surface — see `unit` below.

rule.title: One colour stays one colour.
rule.body:
Violet is the only accent. Amber appears once in a whole artefact, as a warning
band, and never as decoration.

rule.title: Mono is the voice.
rule.body:
Every label, ID and readout is JetBrains Mono, uppercase, tracked. The sans face
never plays instrument. Sizes differ per surface because reading distance does.

rule.title: No fake data.
rule.body:
Every identifier, hash and count is real or is plainly a placeholder. A barcode
is a pattern, never a code that pretends to scan.

website.label: Website
website.what: Live DOM. The Astro site, docs, partners, projects, and the platform apps.
website.unit: the viewport — and the viewport varies, so check at 375 and at 1440
website.basis: verified — read from the website token package and the running site
can: custom properties resolving at runtime, so one drawing serves every ground
cannot: assume the viewer will interact at all
rules: Anything interactive must look interactive before it is touched.
Reduced motion settles with no travel — the parts arrive where they belong.
An accent that only appears on hover is invisible to a third of visitors. It may enrich, never carry.

presentation.label: Presentation
presentation.what: Fixed 1920x1080 .dc.html, exported to PDF, PPTX and PNG.
presentation.basis:
verified for geometry and export path — the deck templates were measured, 120x140
padding and the 92/40/27 type observed. The raster claims below are engineering
reasoning and have NOT been checked against a real PPTX export.
can: a ground chosen per slide by the author, rather than by a viewer
a whole slide given to one object
cannot: hover, focus or active — every state must be the resting state
carry its reveal animation into the PDF or the PPTX
rely on the viewer scanning at their own pace on a projected deck
rules: The 14px chrome step is unreadable from the back of a room. Nothing below 19px carries meaning on this surface.
A hairline survives a PDF; it does not reliably survive a PPTX raster. Structural lines export at 1.5px minimum.
Anything that would have been a hover state becomes either the resting state or a second slide.
The five-layer raised shadow is fine on screen and flattens in export. Do not let elevation carry meaning here.

video.label: Video
video.what: 1920x1080 HTML frames captured to MP4. The explainer pipeline and Remotion.
video.basis:
verified for geometry and type — the frames were measured, 86/34/24 observed.
The compression claims are engineering reasoning about H.264 and have NOT been
measured against a real encode. Treat them as the thing to test first.
can: motion as the information rather than as decoration
a value that changes over time, honestly, with no interaction
building a figure one element per beat
cannot: let the viewer re-read, pause or scan
show anything meaningful for less than about a second
rules: Time is the constraint the other surfaces do not have. If it cannot be read in the time it is up, it is not on the screen.
An identifier needs longer than a word. Truncate a hash to eight characters; never scroll one.
No repeating pattern finer than roughly 32px pitch, and no 1px high-contrast line — fine high-frequency detail is what a codec spends its bitrate on and then loses.
Grain competes with the encoder for the same bits. Expect to run it lower here than the 0.62 the site uses, and measure rather than guess.
Motion must carry meaning. A part that moves for atmosphere is the video equivalent of a sticker.

accent.name: Numeral as object
accent.physical: The number on a hangar door, a part bin, a ticket. It is the biggest thing because it is what you find things by.

website.becomes: Section markers, large and at low contrast. One per section, never inside a card.
website.overuse: Two large numerals in one viewport, or a numeral that counts nothing.

presentation.becomes: The slide's own number, as the object — set large in a corner, or bled off the edge. It is the strongest cheap way to make a deck feel built rather than typed.
presentation.overuse: A numeral on a slide that is not part of a run. A single slide has nothing to count.

video.becomes: A chapter or shot number on a title card. It may count up as the transition itself, which is the one place the numeral can move.
video.overuse: A numeral that changes faster than it can be read. Under about a second it is a flicker, not a number.

accent.name: Part and log IDs
accent.physical: The stamp on a component. It says this is a specific thing, and it can be traced.

website.becomes: Anywhere a real identifier exists — a feature, a run, a hash. Long values truncate.
website.overuse: Invented IDs. An ID on something with no identity in the product.

presentation.becomes: The same, at 19px or above. A hash is truncated to eight characters and the full value goes in the notes — nobody reads 64 characters from a slide.
presentation.overuse: A full hash set at chrome size because it fits. It fits and it cannot be read.

video.becomes: Eight characters, held still, on screen long enough to read. It earns its place when the point is that the thing is traceable.
video.overuse: A scrolling or typing-on ID. The effect reads as a hacker film and the value cannot be read at any frame.

accent.name: Spec plate
accent.physical: The rating plate riveted to a machine: label, value, nothing else.

website.becomes: Four facts that want to be read in a second. The hand-off section, a build run, the OS page.
website.overuse: Plates for prose. A plate with a sentence in it is a table wearing a costume.

presentation.verdict: yes — the strongest of the thirteen here
presentation.becomes: A whole slide can be a spec plate, up to about six rows. It is the most honest way a deck states facts, and it needs no illustration.
presentation.overuse: More than six rows, or two plates on one slide. At that point it is a table and should be a table.

video.becomes: One row per beat, arriving in reading order. The build is what gives the viewer the pace they cannot set themselves.
video.overuse: All rows at once. On a page the reader scans; in a shot they cannot, and a full plate flashed up is a wall.

accent.name: Tick scale
accent.physical: A ruler on the edge of a drawing. It gives the object a size and the reader a position.

website.becomes: Beside a figure, marking a real quantity — requirements traced, files emitted, progress through a run. It may follow scroll.
website.overuse: A scale that measures nothing, or one on every card.

presentation.becomes: Held at one value, with that value also stated in words. A reader cannot hover to find out what the mark means.
presentation.overuse: A scale whose value is only readable from its position. On a projected slide, position is approximate.

video.becomes: It animates to its value, and the animation IS the information. A count arriving is more legible in motion than as a number that was always there.
video.overuse: Animating for its own sake, or ending on a value the shot never states.

accent.name: Registration marks
accent.physical: Printer's crosses that align the plates. They say something precise was placed here.

website.becomes: The corners of a product shot or a placeholder. A replacement for the corner brackets, not an addition to them.
website.overuse: Crosses on text blocks. Crosses and brackets together.

presentation.becomes: The corners of the slide's image area — and they double as the visible edge of the safe margin, which is useful on a surface that has one.
presentation.overuse: Crosses on every slide. They mark a placed image, not a page.

video.becomes: Only at 2px or heavier. A 1px cross is exactly the high-frequency detail an encoder discards, and it will crawl.
video.overuse: Any 1px cross. Also crosses that move — a registration mark that travels is not registering anything.

accent.name: Construction lines
accent.physical: The engineer's drawing behind the object: datums, arcs, centre lines. The object was designed, not dropped.

website.becomes: Behind a render or the rings. Drawn in the drafting weights.
website.overuse: Lines behind text. Lines unrelated to the object's geometry.

presentation.becomes: Behind the slide's object. Strong here, because a slide is already a composed frame and the lines give it a reason to be composed that way.
presentation.overuse: Construction lines as a background texture on a text slide.

video.becomes: The lines DRAW IN, then the object appears on them. It shows the object being designed, which is the argument the whole brand makes, in the one medium that can show a sequence.
video.overuse: Drawing in lines that the object then ignores. If the geometry does not match, the sequence is a lie the viewer can see.

accent.name: Leader captions
accent.physical: The callout on an exploded drawing: a line from the part to its name.

website.becomes: From a part to its name — the exploded rings, a build-output figure naming the requirement above the code it produced.
website.overuse: Leaders to things that already have a label under them.

presentation.becomes: The same, and the leaders set the reading order of the slide. A reader follows them in the order they are drawn.
presentation.overuse: More than about four on a slide. Past that the leaders become the subject.

video.becomes: Leaders arriving one per beat is the natural build, and each one buys the viewer the time to read the label at its end.
video.overuse: All leaders at once, or leaders that arrive faster than their labels can be read.

accent.name: Dot grid
accent.physical: Perforated metal, a drilled plate, a notebook cover. A surface with a pitch.

website.becomes: Behind a render or the rings, faded toward one corner. Not on cards with text — that was tried and it fought the grain.
website.overuse: Full-bleed grids. Grids behind reading text.

presentation.becomes: Behind a slide's object, faded. Safe here because the surface is fixed and the pitch can be set once.
presentation.overuse: A grid on a slide that has no object on it.

video.becomes: Only at a coarse pitch. The site's 22px grid is fine high-frequency detail and will alias and crawl through an encode.
video.overuse: The web pitch reused unchanged. It is the single most likely thing on this list to look broken in a finished video.

accent.name: Rotated edge label
accent.physical: The label on a spine, the number on the flank of a vehicle. Read from the side, because that is where you are.

website.becomes: The left edge of a large card or figure, once per section at most.
website.overuse: Rotated body copy. More than one rotated label in view.

presentation.becomes: The left edge of the slide. It is a good way to carry a section name through a run of slides without spending the headline on it.
presentation.overuse: A rotated label carrying anything the slide actually needs read. It is orientation, not content.

video.becomes: Only if it holds still for the whole shot. Rotated type that moves cannot be read at any frame.
video.overuse: A rotated label on a moving or transitioning element.

accent.name: Hazard band
accent.physical: The tape on a step, the stripe on a tail fin. A boundary you must notice.

website.becomes: The beta mark, or a draft build's state. The one place amber may appear.
website.overuse: Stripes as pattern. Two of them anywhere.

presentation.becomes: A state slide: draft, not for distribution, pre-production. One deck, one band.
presentation.overuse: A band on every slide of a draft deck. Once is a warning; every slide is a wallpaper.

video.becomes: Amber survives an encode well, because the stripe is broad and low-frequency. It is the safest strong mark on this surface.
video.overuse: A band that animates. A hazard stripe is a boundary, and a boundary that moves is not one.

accent.name: Tear line
accent.physical: The perforation on a ticket. Two parts that were one thing, and can be separated.

website.becomes: The join between a specification and what was cut from it — the hand-off, the export, the CSV that leaves.
website.overuse: As a section divider. The page has just removed its lines; this would be a fancier line.

presentation.becomes: The split between what was specified and what was produced, on one slide. It can also be the slide boundary itself in a two-part build.
presentation.overuse: A perforation between two things that were never one thing.

video.becomes: The transition tears along the perforation. It is the one transition in this list that means something: the artefact separating into its parts.
video.overuse: Using it as a general-purpose wipe between unrelated shots.

accent.name: Barcode as pattern
accent.physical: The mark that lets a machine read what a person reads. On a screen it can only be texture, honestly.

website.becomes: A small faded area on an export or package figure. Never with digits under it.
website.overuse: A barcode implying it scans to something. Barcodes on cards.

presentation.becomes: The same. Small, faded, on a figure about something leaving the system.
presentation.overuse: A barcode at slide scale. Large, it stops being texture and starts claiming to be a code.

video.becomes: Nothing. A 1-to-3px repeating vertical pattern is the worst case for an encoder — it is pure high-frequency detail with no motion, and it will smear and pulse.
video.overuse: Any use at all on this surface. If a package needs marking, use the ID instead.

accent.name: Coordinate readout
accent.physical: The instrument reading: where the thing is right now. Live, tabular, exact.

website.becomes: Attached to a figure, showing one requirement's real position in the output. It may update as the reader interacts.
website.overuse: Readouts of invented values. The cyber-brutalist coordinate for its own sake.

presentation.becomes: A frozen reading, carrying a run id or a timestamp so it is honestly a snapshot. Nothing is live on a slide, and a readout that implies it is, lies.
presentation.overuse: A readout marked live, or with a state like Running, on a surface where nothing runs.

video.verdict: yes — the one honest live case
video.becomes: It may tick and update as the shot plays. This is the only surface where a value can change without the viewer acting, so it is the only place `live` is true without interaction.
video.overuse: Values ticking faster than they can be read, or a readout that changes with no cause shown in the shot.
